The system of OPC UA already provides means to express the semantic of an OPC UA Object. As an example, IEC 62541-100 defines the DeviceType ObjectType expressing that instances of this ObjectType represent devices. Subtypes of the DeviceType are used to add vendor specific semantic. However, the classification and additional semantic of the device in terms of an external data dictionary is not specified further. This document provides means to represent that an Object is for example a differential pressure transmitter in the context of an IEC Common Data Dictionary. This allows clients to automatically retrieve and identify such devices.

This document is an integral part of the IEC 62541 series, that is, the types defined in this document shall be used as defined. However, it is not required but strongly recommended that a Server use the types defined in this document to refer to external dictionaries. The defined types can be subtyped to refine their behaviour.

When a Server references external dictionaries using the types defined in this document, it refers from OPC UA Nodes to dictionary entries. The Server can optionally also provide the hierarchy and content of the external dictionary. Resource consumption should be considered, especially in scenarios where the OPC UA Server is part of the firmware of a device.

4.2 Overview

The types and instances defined in this document are illustrated in Figure 1. The DictionaryEntryType is an abstract base type for dictionary entries. The IrdiDictionaryEntryType and the UriDictionaryEntryType provide concrete types that can be used to represent dictionary entries. The HasDictionaryEntry ReferenceType is used to refer an OPC UA Node to a dictionary entry. The DictionaryFolderType and the Dictionaries Object provide an optional capability to expose the hierarchy of a referenced dictionary.

value of 11 values a through z and 0 through 9. This table shows a progressive numbering system from a to p, with each letter representing a different value from 0 to 9. The table continues in this pattern for each subsequent character, until the end of the alphabet.

The first letter in the table is I, which corresponds to the value 49. The second letter is J, which corresponds to the value 50. The third letter is K, which corresponds to the value 51, and so on.

This system of letter-by-letter numbering is used to represent integers in two's complement notation. Two's-complement notation is a method for representing signed numbers using a single array of bits. In two's complement notation, the sign bit is used to represent the sign of the number.

In the first three rows of the table, the sign bit is set to zero (0), indicating a positive number. In the fourth row, the sign bit is set to one (1), indicating a negative number. The last row in the table uses a two's complement notation, with the sign bit set to zero (0) and the two's complement value stored in the array.

The diagram of the iodine content in different foods displayed provides a practical example of how two's complement notation is used in representation of data, especially in determining the value for a specific character such as letter 'I' in the alphabet. Two Fishing was stored in alternating 'A' and 'B' strings, and used to find the lowest index of letter 'I' in the string 'IEEE Spectrum'.

The table structure in the diagram is made structure for the string `"IEEE Spectrum"`. This shows that node [i] is equal to node[i+1], and that the value of node[i+1] is equal to node[i+2], and so forth, until node[2]. the node () marks the end of the table.

In the "i" position, if I is the last letter in a row, then the corresponding node in the "Value" string will be equal to 0, unless this is the last value in the row. Similarly, in the "I" position, if I is the first letter in a row, then the corresponding node in the "Value" string will be equal to 1. The diagram also includes a blank space: "_" (and a hyphen in between) meaning 'the entire rest of the string, including up to but not including this character'. This structure further emphasizes the main purpose of a two's complement notation: to be able to represent characters of text strings with non-empty sets.

The demonstration of iodine content in different foods using two's complement is a practical example of how two's complement notation is used in data representation, especially in determining the value of a specific character like the first line of letter "I" in the alphabet ``IEEE Spectrum``.

In conclusion, two's complement notation is a method of representing numbers where the sign bit is used to represent the sign of the number, and two's complement values are used to represent the position of a specific character in a number, providing a standardized way of representing data for understanding and manipulation.

5.4 URI based dictionary entry type

The UriDictionaryEntryType defined in Table 4 is used to represent dictionary entries that use URIs as unique identifiers.

Table 4 – UriDictionaryEntryType definition

| Attribute                           | Value |
|-----------------------------------|-------|
| BrowseName                          | UriDictionaryEntryType |
| IsAbstract                          | False |
| References                         | NodeClass | BrowseName    | DataType / TypeDefinition  | ModellingRule |
| Subtype of the DictionaryEntryType defined in 5.1. |           |
|                                               |           |
|                                               | Conformance Units |

Address Space Dictionary URI

The identifier in the respective external dictionary shall be a unique URI string. This identifier is used for the $NodeId$ and the $BrowseName$ Attributes of instances of the $DictionaryEntryType$. The $IdentifierType$ of the $NodeId$ shall be $STRING\_1$ with the identifier from the external dictionary as the value.

The namespace "http://opcfoundation.org/UA/Dictionary/URI" shall be used for instance of the URI $DictionaryEntryType$. Subtypes can define different namespaces.

The identifier shall be immutable; meaning that it shall not be reassigned to a different dictionary entry within the scope of the namespace in future versions. Data dictionaries can be publicly defined by standard bodies such as IEC or proprietary (e.g. vendor-specific dictionaries).

6 HasDictionaryEntry ReferenceType

The HasDictionaryEntry ReferenceType is a concrete $ReferenceType$ and can be used directly. It is a subtype of $NonHierarchicalReferences$.

The $Reference$ to the dictionary entry for any $Node$ is provided by $HasDictionaryEntry$.

The $SourceNode$ of this $ReferenceType$ can be any $Node$. The $TargetNode$ of this $ReferenceType$ shall be an $Object$ of $DictionaryEntryType$ or one of its subtypes.

Each $Node$ can be the $SourceNode$ of multiple $HasDictionaryEntryReferences$ pointing to multiple dictionary entry $Objects$.

The $HasDictionaryEntryReferenceType$ is specified in Table 5.

The normal approach of associating DictionaryEntryType Nodes with HasDictionaryEntry References cannot be used with a MultistateValueDiscreteType Variabletype due to the EnumValues Property being an Array, making this Type necessary. References can however be used for other VariableTypes. For example, the TwoStateDiscreteType can use HasDictionaryEntry References with SourceNode being the TrueState and FalseState Properties and Targetnode being the DictionaryEntryNodes.

EnumDictionaryEntries is a two-dimensional array of Nodeds. The first dimension is used to list all possible dictionary entry values for the related variable in a specific dictionary (e.g., CDD or ECLASS). The second dimension is used to reference this dictionary. The size of the first array dimension shall be the same size as the EnumValues Property.

ValueAsDictionaryEntries provides a list of all dictionary entry values in the different dictionaries related to the current value of the variable. The order of the array entries shall be in the same order used by the EnumDictionaryEntries Property.

transitions as binary segments compete for dominance. Figure 5 shows an example of this relationship using a sequence of transitions between states in a lexical database for Latin words.

When there are multiple transitions for a given letter, Weiner picks the longest transition corresponding to a letter. For example, if LiSee Statrie is printed and weit and sieben (Sehr or兴奋) are available for it, the transition [sehr,sieben] is chosen instead.

In general, we find that Weiner’s algorithm fails for highly inflected words, such as German words and German words with French suffixes.

The method’s major weakness is that may not be able to pick the transition corresponding to an inflected word as well as pure positional transitions. This all results in fewer available transitions per character, which can possibly lead to misrecognitions, such as “se, sie, seh” and “sir, siv” being rendered as a single transition throughtout the text.

The paper reaffirms the fact that automatic text discerning is a challenging task. The two methods that were used are not perfect, and further work is needed to improve such methods and eventually transform part of the industrial production of text to extract characters and words of today's computer system. The methods can be used in different ways depending on specific requirements. Early classification for less accurate purposes, such as sorting texts according to user's wishes. They can be used as auxiliary tools during the refining work of authoring for multitude of causes, such as ensuring that multiple sources indicate the same content.

This work, therefore, represents a major step forward in the fact that the computer system is capable of identifying the character of texts that know previous transcripts in the language.
